name: Fenway Park
label: Fenway Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jersey Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jersey Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11188464: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fenway Park' (329 m across).
notes: Home of the Red Sox with the Green Monster wall.

text.description: Fenway Park is the home of the Boston Red Sox and the oldest active ballpark in Major League Baseball. The first game was played on 20 April 1912. The park was substantially rebuilt in 1934, when the Green Monster, the tall left-field wall, took its present form at 37 feet high, painted in the dark Dartmouth Green you still see today. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2012. The ballpark is squeezed into a dense city block, so the best outside views are close-up and street-level, which suits a phone well. From there you get the entrance gate with the Red Sox logo, framed by the street and its banners. The address was once Yawkey Way, but the street went back to its original name, Jersey Street, in 2018. If you have time, two other free outside views are worth a look. Lansdowne Street shows the Green Monster wall rising above the road. The bronze Teammates statue of four Red Sox players stands in front of the ballpark. Inside the park, including the Green Monster seats, you need a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Fenway Park is in Boston's dense Fenway–Kenmore neighbourhood, close to Kenmore Square. The block is bordered by Brookline Avenue, Jersey Street, Van Ness Street and Lansdowne Street.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Kenmore Square, then head for Jersey Street beside the ballpark. The address is 4 Jersey Street; use a map app to navigate from Kenmore Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the gate and the street together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back. Use 2x zoom for a tighter shot of the Red Sox logo.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jersey Street (across from the main gate at 4 Jersey St). The Fenway Park entrance gate with the Red Sox logo, framed by the street. Across from the main gate at 4 Jersey Street, with the ballpark to the east. From here the photo shows the Fenway Park entrance gate with the Red Sox logo, framed by the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the gate centred, with the street leading into the frame and the banners along the sides. Keep your phone level so the gate and building edges stay straight. For a different view, walk to Lansdowne Street for the Green Monster wall above the road, or to the Teammates statue with the stadium behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate or logo to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the signs and colours stay rich. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, outside game hours, is likely to be easier for a clear view of the gate. Before games the street can be busy, so allow extra time and patience.

text.access_note: The Jersey Street viewpoint is an outside public street, but entry to the ballpark itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Jersey Street is reported by one guide to be closed to vehicles for about three hours before games, so it can be crowded; current closures were not checked.
Daytime outside game hours is likely to be quieter than before a game.
Lansdowne Street and the Teammates statue are free outside views near the ballpark; the statue's exact location was not checked against official sources.
Interior areas such as the Green Monster seats and Pesky's Pole need a ticket.

name: USS Constitution
label: USS Constitution
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piers Park' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piers Park' (way/29745239): middle (532 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/166151194: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'USS Constitution' (68 m across).
notes: World's oldest commissioned warship afloat.

text.description: USS Constitution, nicknamed Old Ironsides, is a three-masted wooden frigate launched in Boston in 1797. She is the oldest naval vessel still afloat, and she is still a commissioned US Navy ship with a crew of 75 officers and sailors. She is usually berthed at Pier 1 of the former Charlestown Navy Yard, at one end of the Freedom Trail. This spot shows her from a distance. The ship looks small from here, so treat this as a wider scene rather than a close portrait. The open water, the Charlestown shoreline and the sky all go into the frame, and the ship becomes a small, recognisable shape within it. It is also a calmer place to stand than some of the busier harbour viewpoints. If you want her at close range with the Boston skyline behind, Pier 1 itself is the alternative. The ship is reported to be closed on Mondays and major holidays, so check current hours before you go. Her sailing cruises are rare, so don't plan around seeing her under sail. Zoom in a little, hold the phone steady against a rail or your body, and take several frames so you can choose the sharpest.
text.geographic_location: The ship is berthed at the Charlestown Navy Yard, on the Charlestown side of Boston Harbour.
text.directions_text: Piers Park is on the East Boston waterfront, across the harbour from the ship's berth at the Charlestown Navy Yard at the end of the Freedom Trail. Check a local map or transit app for the nearest station or stop, and head for the waterfront park. Once there, face north-west across the harbour to find the ship, about 1.9 km away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide harbour scene, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the ship closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piers Park (East Boston waterfront, looking west across the harbor). The ship from a greater distance across the harbor, useful for a wider frame that takes in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the shoreline on a lower line so the water and sky sit calmly around the ship. Keep the ship off-centre, on one of the grid crossings, rather than in the middle. The ship will look small, so let the water be part of the picture. For a closer view with the skyline behind, Pier 1 is the alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the ship to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so it does not wash out. Take a few frames at 2x-5x, resting your elbows on a rail or bench to keep it sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The light depends on the time of day and the weather. Aim to have the sun behind or beside you rather than in front of you.

text.access_note: Piers Park is a free public park. The ship is a working Navy vessel that welcomes visitors, but check the official site before you go for current hours.

name: Prudential Tower
label: Prudential Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Copley Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Copley Square' (way/1239199995): middle (190 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q606823: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Skyscraper with the Skywalk Observatory.

text.description:
The Prudential Tower, known locally as the Pru, is a 52-floor glass-and-aluminium tower in Boston's Back Bay. It was completed in 1964 and is 749 feet (228 m) tall, or 907 feet (276 m) including its radio mast. That makes it the second-tallest building in the city, after the John Hancock Tower. When it opened, it ended the Custom House Tower's long run as Boston's tallest building. It stands at the heart of the Prudential Center complex at 800 Boylston Street, with a shopping mall in its base.

It photographs well because it is a plain, upright shape that gives the skyline a clear anchor. From Copley Square, the tower rises above the Back Bay streets and the square's buildings, so you can show the city and the tower together. Its windows are sometimes lit to spell out messages for local sports teams and charity events, which is worth a look if you are here after dark.

For a phone shot, include some foreground, such as the square's buildings or trees, so the tower has scale. Keep the phone upright and level, and turn on gridlines to help keep the vertical lines straight. If you want a different view, the Longfellow Bridge looks across the Charles River to the Prudential Center cluster, and the riverbank across the water shows it beside the Hancock tower.
text.geographic_location: The Prudential Tower is in the Back Bay district of Boston, at the centre of the Prudential Center complex. The complex is bordered by Belvidere, Dalton, Boylston and Exeter streets.
text.directions_text: Head for Copley Square in Back Bay. The tower is about 580 m (a short walk) to the south-west of the square. Once you are on the Boylston Street side of the square, look south-west and the tower will be above the rooftops. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the tower and the buildings around Copley Square in one frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, and keep the phone level so the tower doesn't lean. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the upper floors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Copley Square (Boylston Street side, looking southwest toward the tower). The Pru rising above the Back Bay streetscape and the Copley Square buildings, with the tower as the main skyline element in the frame. Face south-west. From here the Pru rises above the Back Bay streetscape and the Copley Square buildings, with the tower as the main skyline feature in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the square's buildings or trees along one edge of the frame and let the tower rise behind them. Turn on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the tower's edge. For a different view, try the Longfellow Bridge, which looks across the Charles River to the Prudential Center cluster.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the glass doesn't wash out. Hold the phone as upright as you can, because tilting it up makes the sides of the tower lean inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest view of the whole tower. If you are here on an evening when a big game is on, the tower's window lights sometimes spell out messages, and night mode will help; rest your elbows on something steady for the longer exposure.

text.access_note: Copley Square is a public square, but the tower is an office and shopping complex, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.

name: Boston Common
label: Boston Common
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Soldiers and Sailors Monument' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Soldiers and Sailors Monument' (node/358277245): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17995454: large area 'Boston Common' (814 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: America's oldest public park.

text.description:
Boston Common is a large public park in the middle of downtown Boston, and it is the oldest city park in the United States. It covers about 50 acres, bounded by Tremont Street, Park Street, Beacon Street, Charles Street and Boylston Street, with the Public Garden next door to the west. In the 1630s the town bought most of this land to use as shared ground, and for a long time cows grazed here. They were formally banned in 1830. Today it is a place of lawns, paths and old trees, and it was made a Boston Landmark in 1977.

For a phone photo, the best-known view is from the Soldiers and Sailors Monument on the small rise of Flagstaff Hill. Face southwest and the Back Bay buildings rise above the tree line, with branches framing the shot. It works best on a clear day. If you have time, Frog Pond gives you the city skyline behind the water, which looks most striking when the pond is an ice rink. Brewer Fountain is a good simple subject when it is running.

The park is big, so you do not need to cover all of it. Pick the hill for the skyline, add one of the other two stops if you fancy it, and keep an eye out for event closures.
text.geographic_location: Boston Common sits in downtown Boston, with the Public Garden immediately to its west. The city's visitor centre is on the Tremont Street side of the park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the edge of the park along Tremont Street, Beacon Street or Charles Street. The view is from the Soldiers and Sailors Monument at the top of Flagstaff Hill, so follow the paths uphill to the monument. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the trees and the buildings together. Try 2x-3x if your phone has telephoto, to bring the Back Bay skyline closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the monument or the open lawns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (top of Flagstaff Hill, looking southwest toward the Public Garden). Back Bay buildings rising above the tree line, framed by the trees near the Common's high point. And look southwest toward the Public Garden. From here you see Back Bay buildings rising above the tree line, framed by the trees near the Common's high point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the skyline on the upper line, letting branches fill the top corners as a natural frame. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. If you want a different view, Frog Pond shows the skyline behind the water, and Brewer Fountain makes a neat single subject when it is running.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the buildings to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Use portrait mode for the fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, and go earlier in the day, ideally before noon, when the light falls well on the buildings. Frog Pond looks best in winter when it is an ice rink.

text.access_note: Boston Common is an open public park, but check the official site before you go in case of event closures.

name: Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum
label: Tea Party Ships
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Congress Street Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Congress Street' (way/85890998): middle (75 m across); moved 40 m off water.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q19024: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Replica ships on Congress Street Bridge.

text.description: The Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum recalls the night of 16 December 1773, when members of the Sons of Liberty, disguised as American Indians, boarded the merchant ship Dartmouth and threw 340 or 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston Harbor. Today the story is told with the replica ships Eleanor and Beaver, moored along Fort Point Channel. They make a good subject because they are full-size, tall-masted and sit against a backdrop of the Boston skyline and the Fort Point warehouses. The best free view is from the sidewalk of the Congress Street Bridge, just outside the museum entrance. From there you can fit the ships, the water and the city into one frame, which works well on a phone held upright or on its side. Keep the ships' masts and rigging clear of the bridge railings and lamp posts, and wait a moment for people to move out of the foreground. If you have time, Congress Street itself is a second angle, with the ships and museum seen against the channel. One guide suggests it is worth trying in the early morning, when the sun rises behind them. Photography is allowed on the ships and open-air decks but not inside the museum, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go aboard.
text.geographic_location: The ships are moored along Fort Point Channel in Boston, beside the Congress Street Bridge and close to the Fort Point warehouses. The museum entrance is right by the bridge.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so from central Boston go by taxi to the Congress Street Bridge over Fort Point Channel. The museum entrance is right outside. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the ships, the channel and the skyline in one frame. Switch to 2x or the telephoto lens to pick out the rigging and masts. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a very big sky, and keep the ships away from the edges of the frame, where they can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Congress Street Bridge (sidewalk on the bridge over Fort Point Channel, facing the moored ships). The replica ships Eleanor and Beaver moored along the channel, with the Boston skyline and Fort Point warehouses behind them. From here the replica ships Eleanor and Beaver sit along the channel, with the Boston skyline and Fort Point warehouses behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the ships along the lower third, with the skyline above and the water leading the eye towards them. Hold the phone level so the masts stay upright, and keep the bridge railing out of the foreground. For a different angle, try Congress Street, where the ships and museum are framed against the channel.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the ships to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the hulls and sails keep their detail. Take a few shots in a row, as people and boats move through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, from the eastern sidewalk, when one guide says the light falls best on the ships. Early morning is an alternative from Congress Street, with the sun rising behind the ships.

text.access_note: The bridge sidewalk is a free outdoor viewpoint. For boarding the ships or entering the museum, check the official site for access and entry details before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Eleanor and Beaver are replica ships moored along Fort Point Channel.
Late afternoon light from the eastern sidewalk of the Congress Street Bridge suits the ships (one guide).
A sunrise view from Congress Street is suggested; check on the day.

name: Acorn Street
label: Acorn Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Acorn Street' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W818143478 (Acorn Street): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Cobblestone lane on Beacon Hill.

text.description:
Acorn Street is a one-block lane that rises uphill between rows of Federal-style brick houses. Gas lamps and cobblestones run the length of it, and together they make the kind of old-fashioned street scene that looks good in a phone photo with very little effort. The lane is short and the buildings line up on both sides, so the eye is carried straight up the slope towards Willow Street.

Guides recommend the view from the bottom, at the West Cedar Street end, looking up the block. From there you get the whole lane in one frame: brick fronts on either side, gas lamps and the cobbles leading upwards. The straight view along the length of the lane between the brick facades is the one most visitors photograph.

People live in these houses and the street is a private way, so be considerate. Keep to the roadway, do not block doorways and avoid pointing your phone into open windows. The cobbles are uneven and can be slippery when wet or icy, so watch your footing while you look at the screen. Casual phone photos do not need a permit; only professional shoots do, through the Acorn Street Association.

Go early in the morning if you can, before the crowds arrive. Late afternoon is also a good time.
text.geographic_location: Acorn Street is a short one-block lane in Boston, running between West Cedar Street and Willow Street.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed near this spot, so walk in via Mount Vernon Street or Willow Street. Acorn Street runs between West Cedar Street and Willow Street. The phone icon on the map marks Acorn Street itself; the best view is at the West Cedar Street end, looking up the block. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the lane much as your eye sees it. The ultra-wide (0.5x) fits more in but can stretch the edges of the buildings, so use it only if you are very close. The telephoto (2x or more) is useful for a tighter shot of the lamps and cobbles climbing the hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Acorn Street at the West Cedar Street end, at the bottom of the block, and look up the lane. From here the whole one-block street rises between the brick row houses, with the gas lamps and cobblestones leading towards Willow Street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the middle of the lane on the centre line so the two rows of houses balance. Keep your phone level so the brick fronts do not lean. The straight view along the length of the lane between the brick facades is the one most visitors photograph, so try it too if you want a second angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick fronts to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the sky and the shaded lane from looking too dark or too bright. Wait a moment for people to move out of the roadway before you take the photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds, is best. Late afternoon is also recommended.

text.access_note: Acorn Street is a private way where residents live, though you can photograph it from the roadway; keep to the roadway and be quiet and considerate. Professional shoots need a permit from the Acorn Street Association.

name: Faneuil Hall
label: Faneuil Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dock Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Dock Square' (node/158814850): point; moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29551702: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Faneuil Hall' (44 m across).
notes: Historic marketplace and meeting hall with the grasshopper weathervane.

text.description:
Faneuil Hall is a red-brick market and meeting hall in the middle of Downtown Boston. It opened in 1742 and was designed by the artist John Smibert. It is often called "the Cradle of Liberty" because of the speeches and debates held inside over the years. Charles Bulfinch enlarged it in 1806, so what you see today is a mix of its original look and later changes.

It photographs well because the front is so clear: arched windows on the ground floor, brick bays divided by pilasters, and a small cupola on top with a grasshopper-shaped weathervane. The open space in front gives you room to step back and fit the whole building into one frame. Passers-by in the foreground add scale and a bit of life.

Keep the facade filling the frame across the open space, with people walking through the lower part of the picture. Dock Square, on the western side of the hall, is the classic view if you want to try a different angle. Nearby, a bronze statue of Samuel Adams stands on the west side of the building and makes a good second subject. If you walk round to the Quincy Market side, you can photograph the hall together with the market buildings. The hall is a stop on the Freedom Trail, so you may find other visitors in your shot, especially in summer.
text.geographic_location: Faneuil Hall stands in Downtown Boston, on the east side of Congress Street, with Boston City Hall across the road and the Quincy Market buildings just to the east.
text.directions_text: Start from Downtown Boston or the Government Center area and head to Faneuil Hall. If you are already walking the Freedom Trail, the hall sits between the Old State House and the Paul Revere House. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close or the square is crowded, and the telephoto (2x or more) for the cupola and weathervane.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Dock Square. The hall's front facade filling the frame across the open square, with pedestrians in the foreground. The hall's front facade fills the frame across the open space, with people walking in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up so its vertical edges follow the grid lines. Keep your phone level so the brick bays don't lean. Leave some square and pedestrians in the lower part of the frame for scale. For a different view, Quincy Market shows the hall alongside the market buildings, and Christopher Columbus Park may offer a view across the street framed by trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour. Wait for a gap in the crowd before pressing the shutter, or take a Live Photo and pick the cleanest moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter, as summer afternoons can be very busy. Around blue hour, when the dome is lit, makes a good scene with Quincy Market. Use night mode and hold your phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The outside of the hall can be photographed from the open public squares around it; if you want to go inside, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day is likely to be quieter than later in the day.
Summer afternoons near the hall can be very crowded (from one guide).
Quincy Market is best framed with the hall at blue hour when the dome is lit (from one guide).
Christopher Columbus Park may give a view across the street toward the hall, though the sightline is not certain.
Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps keep vertical lines straight.

name: Boston Public Library
label: Boston Public Library
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Copley Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Copley Square' (way/1239199995): middle (190 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/63755: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Boston Public Library' (199 m across).
notes: Palazzo-style library on Copley Square.

text.description: The Boston Public Library's Central Library stands on Copley Square in Back Bay, and its Beaux-Arts front is one of the easiest big buildings in the city to photograph. The square gives you open space to stand back, so the whole façade fits in one frame. Trinity Church and the glass Hancock Tower are close enough to appear beside it, which makes a good then-and-now picture of Boston. The library was authorised by a Massachusetts statute in 1848 and officially established by a city ordinance in 1852. Its Reading Room opened in 1854 in a former schoolhouse on Mason Street. The Copley Square building was designated a Boston Landmark in 2000, and the library holds around 24 million items, making it the third-largest public library in the United States. For the classic wide shot, stand in Copley Square across Boylston Street from the main façade and take in the full width of the building. If you have time, walk round to the Dartmouth Street entrance for a second picture. Its arched doors and the sculpture on the steps work well shot head-on, or from the steps looking along the front. The square sometimes hosts events and a farmers market in season, which can block the view, so allow time to move along and find a clear gap.
text.geographic_location: The library is in Back Bay, on the edge of Copley Square, with its main front facing Boylston Street. Trinity Church and the Hancock Tower are close by on the same square.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Back Bay and Copley Square, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. Once in the square, look for the library's long Beaux-Arts front across Boylston Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the library, Trinity Church and the Hancock Tower together. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner shot of the library front alone. A telephoto/zoom lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for the arched doors and the sculpture on the steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Copley Square (across Boylston Street from the library's main McKim façade). The library's Beaux-Arts façade framed in a wide architectural shot, with Trinity Church and the glass Hancock Tower often visible nearby. Across Boylston Street from the library's main McKim façade. From here the Beaux-Arts front fills the frame, with Trinity Church and the glass Hancock Tower often visible nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the façade up with the horizontal lines so the building stands straight. Leave a little space around the edges so you are not cutting off the roofline. Trinity Church or the Hancock Tower can sit to one side as a second subject. For a different view, go to the Dartmouth Street entrance and shoot the arched doors and steps head-on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the library front to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is washing out. Keep your phone level, as tilting it makes tall buildings look as if they are leaning.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the library front is in shade and the light is softer.

text.access_note: The outside of the library can be photographed from public ground, but check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or take photos there.

name: King's Chapel
label: King's Chapel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tremont Street and School Street corner' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Tremont Street and School Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29551954: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kings Chapel' (53 m across).
notes: Granite church on the Freedom Trail.

text.description: King's Chapel is a solid granite church standing at the corner of Tremont Street and School Street. It photographs well because the front is built from heavy stone blocks, with a row of tall columns that give you strong lines and plenty of texture. The congregation began in 1686 as the first Anglican church in colonial New England. The current stone building was designed by Peter Harrison, begun in 1749 and completed in 1754. It was built around the earlier wooden church, which was then taken out through the new windows. Plans for a steeple were dropped when money ran short, which is why the building looks sturdy and flat-topped rather than tall and spired. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1960. Next door is King's Chapel Burying Ground, which is older than the chapel by more than a century, and the chapel also adjoins Old City Hall. The classic angle is from the street corner at the front, facing the entrance. From there you can catch the columns on one side and, looking down the street, the steeple of Park Street Church. Stand back far enough to keep the columns straight, and keep passers-by on the pavement out of the lower edge of the frame. If you would like a second picture, the burying ground gives you weathered slate headstones in the foreground with the chapel walls behind.
text.geographic_location: King's Chapel is in central Boston, at the corner of Tremont Street and School Street. It sits beside Old City Hall and King's Chapel Burying Ground.
text.directions_text: Aim for the corner of Tremont Street and School Street, where the chapel stands. The spot data lists no nearby stations or tram stops, so use a map app to reach that corner. Look for the granite front and the columns. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if pavement or traffic stops you stepping back, and keep the chapel away from the edges, where straight lines can lean. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the column tops, the stonework, or Park Street Church's steeple down the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Tremont Street and School Street (corner at the chapel's front, facing the entrance). The granite Georgian facade and front columns of the chapel, framed from the street corner. From here you see the granite Georgian facade and its front columns framed from the street corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so the building looks upright. Keep the columns on one side of the frame and leave room down the street for Park Street Church's steeple. For a second picture, try King's Chapel Burying Ground, with the old slate headstones in the foreground and the chapel walls behind. Keep to the paths there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone front to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the granite keeps its detail. If people walk through the shot, take a few frames, or hold the shutter button for a burst, and pick the cleanest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light, or a bright overcast day, shows the texture of the granite best. Early in the day there are usually fewer people on the pavement.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but opening times and rules for the chapel interior, including photography and any tours, can change, so check the official site before you go; in the burying ground, keep to the paths.

Soft morning or late-afternoon light, or bright overcast, suits the granite facade.

name: Quincy Market
label: Quincy Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Custom House Tower' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Custom House Tower' (way/29719177): middle (59 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29573399: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Quincy Market' (169 m across).
notes: Domed granite food hall beside Faneuil Hall.

text.description:
Quincy Market is a long, low granite market building in Downtown Boston, finished in 1826 and designed by Alexander Parris. It is the central of three buildings. A domed middle section and a porticoed end on each side give it a calm, symmetrical shape, and the North and South Market buildings stand either side of it. Since 1976 the whole group has been the Faneuil Hall Marketplace, and it is a stop on the Freedom Trail.

From the street it is busy and close-up. The best overall picture comes from above. From up there you can see how the three buildings sit in a row, which is hard to judge at ground level.

If you also want a ground-level shot, walk over to the market. The granite front with its colonnade works well with street performers and passers-by in the frame. Inside, the central rotunda and food hall are lively but crowded, so be considerate of stallholders and other visitors when you take photos. The paved pedestrian streets between the buildings are open and easy to walk, which helps if you want a wide view.
text.geographic_location: Quincy Market is in Downtown Boston on Merchants Row, right beside Faneuil Hall.
text.directions_text: There are no public-transport stops listed for this spot. Quincy Market is one block north of the Custom House. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view from the deck. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the skyline, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the three market roofs and Faneuil Hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Custom House Tower (observation deck, looking down on the market). An elevated aerial view of the three Quincy Market roofs with Faneuil Hall beside them and the skyline behind. At Custom House Tower, on the observation deck, looking down on the market. The roofs of the three Quincy Market buildings lie below you with Faneuil Hall alongside and the skyline behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the three roofs up with a grid line so they sit straight. Keep some skyline in the top third. Telephoto gives a tighter picture of the roofs, while the default lens (1x) shows how they sit in the city. For a ground-level alternative, photograph the granite front and colonnade from the street, or the central dome inside the food hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roofs to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone close to the glass, if there is any, to reduce reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour after sunset, when the city lights come on, is one guide's suggestion. Use night mode if the phone offers it and brace your elbows on a ledge to keep it steady.

text.access_note: The Custom House observation deck is described as open to the public, but check the official site before you go for admission and opening times; the market's streets and food hall are a working public marketplace.
claims_not_in_sources: Quincy Market is about one block north of the Custom House (the sources say the Custom House is one block to the south of the market).
Glass on an observation deck can cause reflections, which holding the phone close to it reduces.
Night mode and bracing your elbows on a ledge help keep low-light phone photos steady.

name: Paul Revere House
label: Paul Revere House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'North Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'North Square' (way/29829944): middle (63 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Paul Revere House'.
notes: Oldest building in downtown Boston.

text.description:
The Paul Revere House is a gabled house with an overhanging upper floor, on North Square in the North End of Boston. It was built no later than 1680, and Paul Revere owned it between 1770 and 1800. It opened as a museum in 1908 after a renovation. It is also the only house on the Freedom Trail, sitting between Faneuil Hall and Old North Church.

It photographs well because it looks so different from what surrounds it. The upper floor overhangs the street, the roof has a gable, and the casement windows add detail to the front. The square's brick surroundings frame the house and make a good backdrop. The best view is of the front, looking south-west towards 19 North Square. A travel guide calls the front a popular photo spot, and old archive photos show the house from the same side of the square.

The square is small and the house is close, so you will probably be taking in the whole front at once. Step back as far as the square allows, keep your phone upright, and let the overhang and gable fill the frame. There is also a brick courtyard beside the house with a bronze bell cast by Revere, which makes a nice second shot if you can see it. Early morning or late afternoon gives the softest light. Photography rules inside the museum may differ, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the North End of Boston, on the north-west side of North Square. It is a short walk from Old North Church along the Freedom Trail.
text.directions_text: Head for the North End and follow the Freedom Trail between Faneuil Hall and Old North Church. The house is at 19 North Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the house. If the square feels too tight to fit the whole front, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). If you have a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the overhang, windows and gable.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in North Square (across the square from the house's front facade, on the 19 North Square side). The front of the two-story gabled house on North Square, with the square's brick surroundings around it. From here you see the whole gabled front with the square's brick surroundings around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the house up with the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. Keep the overhang and gable in the frame and include some of the brick around the house for context. Take one wide shot with the default lens (1x), then a closer one with the telephoto if you have one. There is no second viewpoint for the house itself, so if the front is busy, wait a moment for a gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the house front to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Keep Live Photos on if you want a short moving clip of people passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: The house is a paid museum, so check the official site before you go for opening details and indoor photography rules; the square outside is an open public space.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the whole front in a tight square.
Keeping the phone upright and using gridlines helps keep the walls from leaning.
The square is fairly small, so you have limited room to step back.
The square may be busy with visitors at times, so you may need to wait for a gap.

name: New England Aquarium
label: New England Aquarium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Central Wharf' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Central Wharf (New England Aquarium)' (way/29861018): middle (224 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.

text.description: The New England Aquarium sits right on Boston's harbour front, on Central Wharf. The main building is a brutalist concrete block that opened in 1969, designed by Peter Chermayeff of Cambridge Seven Associates. The glass-and-steel West Wing was added in 1998, so the old and new styles sit side by side. That mix of rough concrete, glass and open water gives you plenty to frame. You don't need to go inside for a good picture. The harbor seal exhibit at the front of the building can be watched for free, at any hour, without entering, so a close shot of the seals makes a good second photo. Next door on Central Wharf is the separate Simons Theatre building. Its facade carries a 2020 mural of a North Atlantic right whale by Shepard Fairey, which is worth a picture of its own. For a different angle, walk along the Boston Harborwalk, where you can catch the building from the waterside path with the outdoor seal exhibit and harbour water in the frame. Take a few frames from each spot and keep the one you like best. Stay back from the water's edge while you compose.
text.geographic_location: On Central Wharf, on Boston's harbour front, with the water on one side and the aquarium's main entrance behind the open plaza.
text.directions_text: Head for Central Wharf on Boston's waterfront. Once you are on the plaza, the facade is only a short step away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and the harbour into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the building. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the seals or for details of the concrete and glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (harbor side, on the Central Wharf plaza in front of the entrance). The aquarium's main facade with the harbor and boats moored beside it, taken from the open plaza. On the harbour-side plaza in front of the entrance. From here the aquarium's main facade is just to the north-east, with the harbour and moored boats beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges lined up with them so the walls don't lean. Put the facade on one side and the water and boats on the other. For a different view, walk the Boston Harborwalk to catch the building from the waterside path with the seal exhibit and harbour in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky or water looks washed out. For the seals, tap on the animal and take a short burst, or try Live Photos so you can pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on concrete and water. Check the weather first, as bright glare on the glass and harbour can be harsh around midday.

text.access_note: The harbor seal exhibit at the front of the building can be viewed from outside for free at any hour.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light on concrete and water.
Bright midday sun can cause glare on glass and harbour water.

name: Old State House
label: Old State House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'State Street at Congress Street' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of State Street and Congress Street (our map tiles).

notes: Colonial landmark surrounded by skyscrapers.

text.description: The Old State House is a small brick building squeezed between modern glass towers in the middle of downtown Boston. Completed in 1713, it is the city's oldest surviving public building. In the 18th century it housed the colonial and state governments, and today it is a history museum. It stood at 65 feet (20 metres), the tallest building in Boston until 1745, so the contrast with the skyscrapers around it is part of the charm. Look up at the gable roof for the lion and unicorn decorations and the tower on top. Just east of the building, a cobblestone marker with a brass ring of stars records the 1770 Boston Massacre. The building is a stop on the Freedom Trail, between the Old South Meeting House and Faneuil Hall. It photographs best from the corner of State Street and Congress Street, where the old façade sits in front of the newer buildings. That is the classic Freedom Trail postcard view. State Street itself gives a wider street-level shot that puts the brick front between the skyscrapers, and Court Street gives a diagonal view that works well as the lights come on at dusk. Plan to take your photos from the pavement, and keep your phone steady. Check the views on the ground, as street layouts and works can change what you see.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of downtown Boston, at 206 Washington Street, where Washington Street meets State Street. It sits on the Freedom Trail between the Old South Meeting House and Faneuil Hall.
text.directions_text: Walk along the Freedom Trail in downtown Boston, or take the MBTA subway to State station, whose entrance is in the building's basement. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the postcard view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the building and the towers behind won't both fit, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the lion and unicorn and the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of State Street and Congress Street (corner from which the building is seen). The Old State House framed as the classic Freedom Trail postcard view, with modern downtown buildings around it. The Old State House is to the west from here, with the modern downtown buildings around it. This is the classic Freedom Trail postcard view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower on the centre line so the building looks upright. Hold the phone level to avoid leaning walls, and leave a little sky above the tower. For a different look, try the wider view from along State Street, where the brick front sits between glass towers. Court Street gives a diagonal view as the lights come on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick façade to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building doesn't go dark. Use night mode at dusk and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: At dusk, when the building's windows glow against the sky.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside from the public pavements, but the museum inside is a ticketed site with limited interior photography, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Phone night mode works well for dusk shots of the building.

name: Bunker Hill Monument
label: Bunker Hill Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Monument Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Monument Square' (way/1263320391): middle (288 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/212124093: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bunker Hill Monument' (16 m across).
notes: Granite obelisk in Charlestown.

text.description:
The Bunker Hill Monument is a granite obelisk on Breed's Hill in Charlestown, where the Battle of Bunker Hill was fought on 17 June 1775. It rises 221 feet (67 m) and was designed by Solomon Willard. It was built between 1825 and 1843 and dedicated on 17 June 1843. When it was finished, it was the largest obelisk in the United States. It stands at the centre of Monument Square Park, a four-acre green space ringed by an avenue of three- and four-storey houses, and it is a stop on the Freedom Trail.

It photographs well because it is so simple. There is one tall, pale shape rising from a green lawn, with trees and landscaping around it and very little to compete with it. The park slopes fairly steeply, with a staircase up from each of its four gates, so you gain a little height as you walk in. A statue of Colonel William Prescott stands to the south of the obelisk and can add some foreground interest. The monument's exterior is lit at night, so an evening shot is possible too.

For the classic picture, stand on the lawn side of Monument Square and turn your phone upright so the full height fits in one frame. Keep the monument central and the gridlines on, because the shaft looks wrong if it leans.
text.geographic_location: The monument is in the Charlestown district of Boston, at the top of Breed's Hill in the middle of Monument Square Park. The Charlestown Navy Yard is roughly a quarter of a mile to the south-east.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so plan your own route to Monument Square in Charlestown, for example on foot along the Freedom Trail. If you are walking the Freedom Trail, this is the last stop after the USS Constitution, and the Charlestown Navy Yard is about a quarter of a mile to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) held upright; from Monument Square it should fit the whole obelisk with some sky above. If you walk closer to the base or want to include the lawn and trees, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone level. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the pointed top and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Monument Square (lawn area around the monument, with the monument filling the frame). The full granite obelisk rising from the green lawn, framed by trees and landscaping. From there the monument is to the north-west. You get the full granite obelisk rising from the green lawn, framed by trees and landscaping.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and put the obelisk in the middle with a little sky above the top. Switch on the gridlines and line up the shaft with a vertical line so it does not appear to lean. Let the trees and lawn fill the lower corners as a natural frame. If you want the Prescott statue in the foreground, move round to the south side and include it at the edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the granite keeps its detail and the sky does not wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a quieter lawn. After dark, the lit exterior suits a night mode shot.

text.access_note: Monument Square is an open public park, but the monument's interior and top may be closed at times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The default lens (1x) held upright should fit the whole obelisk from the stand-here point, which is roughly 100 m away.
The ultra-wide (0.5x) is useful closer to the base of the monument.
Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and the lawn is usually quieter at those times.
The monument's interior and top may be closed at times, so visitors should check before going.

name: Massachusetts State House
label: Massachusetts State Ho
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Boston Common' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Boston Common' (relation/17995454): edge nearest the subject (812 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29718019: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Massachusetts State House' (223 m across).
notes: Golden-domed capitol on top of Beacon Hill.

text.description:
The Massachusetts State House sits at the top of Beacon Hill, with its gold dome and red-brick front looking down over Boston Common. Charles Bulfinch designed it, and it was completed in January 1798. It is one of the oldest state capitols still in use. The dome was first covered in copper in 1802 by Paul Revere's company and was gilded in 1874. It was re-gilded in 23k gold in 1997, and a gilded wooden pine cone sits on top. The building stands in 6.7 acres of grounds, with statues scattered along the front lawns.

It photographs well because the Common gives you open space to step back, so the whole building and its dome fit in one frame with lawns and trees in front. The best view is from the park side across Beacon Street. The lower part of the Common, near the fountain, gives a classic view up the hill to the dome. For a closer shot of the front and steps, walk to the corner of Beacon Street where the State House meets the Common. Use the statues and the Common's trees to add depth. If you want a distant skyline version, Longfellow Bridge looks across the Charles River towards Beacon Hill, and a zoom helps pick out the dome.
text.geographic_location: The State House is on top of Beacon Hill, in central Boston, directly opposite Boston Common on Beacon Street.
text.directions_text: Start from Boston Common, the big park in the middle of the city, and head to its Beacon Street edge, where the State House stands on the hill to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole State House, the dome and the Common's lawns in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the dome and pine cone, especially from further away. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close on the Beacon Street corner and want the full front and steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Boston Common (across Beacon Street from the State House; lower Common by the fountain for an uphill view). The gold dome and white columns rising above the Common's lawns and trees, framed from the park side across Beacon Street. Across Beacon Street from the State House. For an uphill view, walk to the lower Common by the fountain: from there the gold dome and white columns rise above the lawns and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the dome on the central vertical line, with lawn or trees filling the foreground. Hold the phone level so the columns do not lean. For a closer shot, go to the Beacon Street corner and frame the facade and steps. Longfellow Bridge is a good second option for a distant skyline shot with the dome among the Beacon Hill buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail against a bright sky. Check for people or traffic at the edges before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon light is suggested for the Beacon Street side in autumn and spring, and in autumn it is worth arriving before 5 PM. Morning light is also mentioned as good for the dome.

text.access_note: Photographing the outside from the public pavements and the Common is free. Interior photography is restricted in some areas and tours may run on weekdays only, so check the official site before you go.

name: Old North Church
label: Old North Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hull Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Hull Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29650592: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Old North Church' (37 m across).
notes: Steeple of the 'one if by land' lanterns.

text.description:
Old North Church, officially Christ Church in the City of Boston, is a white-steepled Georgian church on Salem Street in the North End. Building began in 1723, and it is the oldest standing church in the city. It is best known for the night of 18 April 1775, when two lanterns were lit in the steeple to warn Patriots of British troop movements before Paul Revere's midnight ride. The steeple rises 191 feet (58 m), and the bell tower holds eight bells cast in 1744, the oldest in North America. The steeple you see today dates from 1955.

It photographs well because of the setting. The church sits on a slope, and from Hull Street the brick front and the tall white steeple line up at the end of the street. The best view is from about halfway up the hill, looking down toward Salem Street. From there you can fit the whole front in one frame. Stand closer and the building is hard to fit in. If you want a second angle, Copp's Hill Burying Ground gives a framed view with the old cemetery to one side. Paul Revere Mall, with the statue of Paul Revere in the foreground, is more casual.

The church is still a working congregation, so go inside only if the doors are open, and check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the North End of Boston, on Salem Street, with Unity Street behind it. On the Freedom Trail it sits between the Paul Revere House and Copp's Hill Burying Ground.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for the North End and look for Salem Street. Copp's Hill Burying Ground gives a view leading down Hull Street to the steeple. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from partway up Hull Street, which takes in the whole front and steeple. Switch to 0.5x only if people or parked cars force you closer. Try 2x to pull the steeple and street together for a tighter shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hull Street (about halfway up the hill, looking down toward Salem Street). The full white-steepled front of the church at the end of the sloping street, with the brick entrance facade visible. That is close, and from close in the building is hard to fit in. For the full-front view, stand partway up Hull Street, about halfway up the hill, and look down toward Salem Street. From there the white-steepled front of the church sits at the end of the sloping street, with the brick entrance facade visible.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the steeple up with a vertical line so it stands straight. Keep the street running down toward the church to lead the eye. For a different shot, go to Copp's Hill Burying Ground and frame the old cemetery on one side with the steeple down the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white steeple to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. Hold the phone level and step back rather than tilting it up, so the building does not lean. Take a few shots in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a time when the sun is not directly behind the steeple, and try to arrive early in the day when the street is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The view from Hull Street is from a public street, but the church is an active congregation with paid tours and visiting hours that vary, so check the official site before you go inside.

name: Boston Public Garden
label: Public Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Make Way for Ducklings' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Charles Street and Beacon Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23787885: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Boston Public Garden' (567 m across).
notes: Lagoon, footbridge and swan boats.

text.description: The Boston Public Garden is a large, tidy park right in the middle of the city, next to Boston Common. It was the first public botanical garden in America. The landscape covers about 24 acres and was designed by George F. Meacham. The pond was finished in 1859, the wrought iron fence went up in 1862, and the suspension bridge over the middle of the pond dates from 1867. For photos it gives you a lot in one place: weeping willows, flower beds, winding paths and the water with the Back Bay skyline in the distance. On this map, start by the bronze duckling statues on the Charles and Beacon Street side. They make a playful, recognisable Boston scene, especially for couples and families. Keep them in the foreground, with the garden's trees and path behind. It is a small spot, so it works best when you wait for a gap in the crowd. For a second picture, walk south to the Lagoon Bridge. Frame the arched footbridge with willow branches and the still water, with the skyline behind. Tulips and magnolias peak from late April into early May, and the willows are lush from late spring through autumn. The bridge gets very crowded from mid-morning, so go early if you want a clear frame.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of Boston, between Beacon Hill to the north and Back Bay to the west, next to Boston Common (to the east), with Boylston Street along the south side. The ducklings are on the Charles Street and Beacon Street side.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed close by, so check a local transit map or walk in from Beacon Hill or Boston Common. Head for the Charles Street and Beacon Street side of the garden and look for the duckling statues; their exact position is approximate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the duckling statues, held low so they sit large against the trees. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the Lagoon Bridge with willow branches overhead. Use 2x if you need to cut out people and focus on the bridge's arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Charles Street and Beacon Street (Near the bronze duckling statues on the Charles and Beacon Street side of the garden). The bronze duckling statues in the foreground with the garden's trees and path behind them. Stand at Make Way for Ducklings, near the bronze duckling statues on the Charles and Beacon Street side of the garden. The middle of the garden, and the lagoon, lie to the south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch so your phone is near statue height, put the ducklings in the lower third and let the path and trees fill the background. Turn on gridlines to keep the line of ducklings level. If you want the lagoon as well, walk south to the Lagoon Bridge. Frame the arched bridge with willow branches and the water as a clean background, with the Back Bay skyline behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statues to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the bronze keeps its detail against the bright path. Portrait mode works well for family pictures beside the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day, before the crowds build, gives the best chance of a clear frame at the statues and the bridge. The bridge is very crowded from mid-morning. Late April to early May brings tulips and magnolias, and the willows look lush from late spring through autumn.

text.access_note: This is an open public garden, but the City of Boston is said to require a permit for professional photo shoots, so check the official site before you go if you plan more than casual phone photos.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone low, at statue height, makes the ducklings look bigger against the background.
Early in the day is likely to be quieter at the statues and the bridge.
Bronze can lose detail against a bright path if the exposure is too high.
The exact position of the duckling statues may differ slightly from the stand-here point, so look for them as you enter the garden.

name: Leonard P. Zakim Bunker Hill Memorial Bridge
label: Zakim Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Paul Revere Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Paul Revere Park' (way/172440085): middle (315 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/508557869: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Leonard P. Zakim Bunker Hill Memorial Bridge' (462 m across).
notes: Cable-stayed bridge over the Charles River.

text.description: The Zakim Bridge carries Interstate 93 over the Charles River at Charlestown. It is a cable-stayed bridge, finished in 2003, and was built as part of the Big Dig. It replaced the older Charlestown High Bridge, a truss bridge from the 1950s. The cables hang from the towers in a harp layout, like the strings of an instrument. The top of each tower is shaped like an obelisk, echoing the Bunker Hill Monument nearby. That clean, repeating shape is what makes it easy to photograph. The Charles River and the bridge deck sit in the frame, and the bridge often shows up as a silhouette. Guides often call this the classic Boston view of the bridge. The park is open, free and has a lawn and a playground, so there is room to move around and try a few angles. The bridge itself is a live highway, so never stand on the roadway, the ramps or the shoulders. Paul Revere Park was being cleared and reworked for a new park, so the view may change. Check current access before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Charlestown, on the north side of central Boston, where Interstate 93 crosses the Charles River. Paul Revere Park lies right beside the bridge, and North Point Park is nearby, linked to Charlestown by the North Bank Bridge.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Charlestown and walk to Paul Revere Park, an open park beside the bridge. Keep to the park paths and lawn, and stay off the roads and ramps around the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the towers, the cables and the river together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full height of a tower and the sweep of the cables from close by. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the obelisk tops or the cable pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Paul Revere Park (eastern end of the park, where the towers rise above the lawn). The bridge's towers and cable harp from the park, often as a silhouette, with the Charles River and the bridge deck in view. At the eastern end where the towers rise above the lawn, and face south-west towards the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place a tower on one of the vertical lines so the cables fan out across the frame. Keep some lawn or water at the bottom to give a sense of place. If you have time, North Point Park is a good second spot for a low, sweeping view of the full span with the skyline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright sky to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little. This keeps the sky colour and turns the towers into a clean silhouette. Use night mode after dark, and hold the phone against a rail or your body to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into evening usually suits the silhouette look, and dusk adds a softer sky behind the cables.

text.access_note: Paul Revere Park is an open, free public park, but the bridge is a live highway, so keep off the roadway and check for any restrictions, especially under the span, before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon into evening usually gives a good sky for a silhouette of the bridge from the park.
Dusk usually gives a softer sky behind the cables.
Looking from the park towards the bridge faces south-west, so the sky behind the towers is often bright in the afternoon and evening.

name: Trinity Church
label: Trinity Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Copley Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Copley Square' (way/1239199995): middle (190 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/64066: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Trinity Church' (100 m across).
notes: Romanesque church mirrored in the Hancock Tower.

text.description:
Trinity Church is the big stone church on Copley Square in Back Bay, and it is one of the best-known landmarks on the square. The congregation dates from 1733, but the present church was built between 1872 and 1877, after the Great Boston Fire destroyed the earlier site on Summer Street. Henry Hobson Richardson designed it, and it is regarded as the birthplace of the Richardsonian Romanesque style, with rough Dedham Granite, heavy arches, coloured stonework and a massive central tower. That tower was designed by Stanford White, who was then working in Richardson's office, and it was based on a tower in Salamanca, Spain.

It photographs well because the church stands in the open, so you can see the whole facade at once. The shallow reflecting pool in front of the church doubles the towers when the water is calm, and the Boston Public Library sits across the square. The square itself is often lively, which adds life to a wide shot.

For the classic picture, stand in Copley Square facing the main facade and let the pool fill the bottom of the frame. If you have time, try the corner of Clarendon Street, where the church's stonework is mirrored in the blue glass of the Hancock Tower. You can also try the library entrance for a straight-on view across the square. Late afternoon gives the warmest light on the stone.
text.geographic_location: Trinity Church is in the Back Bay district of Boston, on Copley Square. The Boston Public Library stands on the opposite side of the square.
text.directions_text: No transit stop is listed for this spot, so head for Copley Square in Back Bay. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both towers and the pool in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the facade. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower, the arches and the stone detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Copley Square (in front of the church, facing its main facade). The church's stone facade with its towers, framed by the shallow reflecting pool in front of it, with the Boston Public Library across the square. From here the church is to the east. You see its stone towers framed by the reflecting pool, with the Boston Public Library across the square. For a different view, try Clarendon Street for the church mirrored in the Hancock Tower's glass, or the library entrance for a straight-on view across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the central tower up with the middle vertical line. Keep the phone level so the towers do not lean. Crouch low near the pool's edge so the water takes up the bottom third and repeats the facade. If the square is busy, wait for a gap or include a few people to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays blue and the stone keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady and wait for calm water if you want a clean reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun sets over Old South Church and warms the stone of the church. One photographer recommends August.

text.access_note: The square and the outside of the church are open to the public, but the interior opening hours vary, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: A calm, windless day gives the clearest reflection in the pool.
Tilting the phone upward, especially on the ultra-wide lens, makes tall towers appear to lean inwards.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the sky from washing out against bright stone.

photo.artist: The original uploader was Daderot at English Wikipedia.

name: Granary Burying Ground
label: Granary Burying Ground
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tremont Street' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Tremont Street and Bromfield Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29861355: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Granary Burying Ground' (160 m across).
notes: Resting place of Paul Revere, Samuel Adams and John Hancock.

text.description: Granary Burying Ground is Boston's third-oldest cemetery, founded in 1660, and it sits on Tremont Street next to Park Street Church and behind the Boston Athenæum. Its tall Egyptian Revival gate and iron fence, designed by Isaiah Rogers, make a ready-made frame, with the iron fence on Tremont Street built in 1840, and rows of weathered slate headstones, old trees and the Park Street Church spire behind. The cemetery holds 2,345 grave-markers, and historians think as many as 5,000 people are buried here. Paul Revere, Samuel Adams, John Hancock, Robert Treat Paine and the five Boston Massacre victims are among them, so it is a stop on the Freedom Trail. Inside, the tall granite obelisk, put up in 1827 for Benjamin Franklin's parents and relatives, is the easiest landmark to spot. The headstones were moved into neat rows in the 19th century, which gives the ground a tidy, repeating pattern that works well in a photo. Take your main picture from the pavement on Tremont Street, opposite the arch, where guides say the best view of the famous graves can be had. Expect other visitors on the pavement, as this stretch is busy with Freedom Trail walkers, so be patient and shoot between groups. Low light makes photography hard here, so aim for daylight. If you go in, the obelisk with its surrounding stones and shade makes a good second picture.
text.geographic_location: Granary Burying Ground is in central Boston, on Tremont Street next to Park Street Church and just north of Boston Common. It lies behind the Boston Athenæum and opposite Suffolk University Law School.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so start from Boston Common or Park Street Church and walk to Tremont Street. From there the middle of the cemetery is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west, and the Park Street Church spire is close by. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole gate arch and the headstones behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people or traffic force you to stand close, and keep the arch near the middle of the frame so its sides don't lean. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for rows of headstones and carved details through the railings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Tremont Street and Bromfield Street (Tremont Street sidewalk at the cemetery's main entrance, opposite the Egyptian Revival arch). The gate arch framing rows of old slate headstones, with the cemetery's trees and the Park Street Church spire nearby. Stand on Tremont Street, on the pavement at the cemetery's main entrance, opposite the Egyptian Revival arch. The middle of the cemetery lies to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the arch up with the central grid line so it looks balanced. Let the headstones fill the gap beneath it, with the church spire above or beside the trees. For a second picture, go inside and shoot the granite obelisk among the weathered gravestones and tree shade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the headstones to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky doesn't wash out and the slate keeps its texture. Avoid night mode here, as dim light makes the cemetery hard to photograph well.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daylight, when the carvings are clear. Choose a quieter moment if you can, because Tremont Street is busy with Freedom Trail foot traffic.

text.access_note: Guides describe the cemetery as free to visit, but opening times can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Quieter moments on the pavement are more likely earlier in the day.
Soft or overcast daylight suits slate headstones and keeps shadows gentle.
